title: Getting the Team to Execute Twice as Fast
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This piece takes on the common pattern of impatient leaders nudging teams to shave small amounts of time off execution, which frustrates everyone and yields little. The author argues the real constraint is expectation, since people stay within what they believe is realistic. The proposed move is to ask an outlandish question, how the team could cut execution time by half, which usually draws incredulity but forces people to drop conventional assumptions. Even when no breakthrough appears, the ideas generated are often better than incremental ones. The closing line, that sometimes leaders must burn the box, sums up a practical provocation to use extreme goals as a tool for creative thinking.
points: Pressing for marginal speed gains breeds resentment and small returns, because it leaves expectations untouched.
Expectations define what people believe is possible, so changing the target is a way to change the thinking.
Asking for a fifty percent cut forces teams to discard assumptions and often surfaces better strategies than incremental tweaks.
Even a failed extreme goal tends to generate stronger ideas than the traditional approach.
quotes: No one enjoys this badgering, including the impatient leader, who is often disappointed by only small gains or none at all. The problem with this picture is not only the leader’s impatience and insistence for a faster pace but also the expectations everyone has about execution.
Expectations frame what is possible. People operate within the limits they perceive are realistic.

Impatient leaders would be much smarter to sit down with those tasked with execution and ask an outlandish question: How can we cut execution time by one-half or more? The reaction is usually swift and incredulous.
Expectations rob people of the creativity they need for out-of-the-box thinking. They also set limits on what is possible, so people avoid looking for more innovative solutions.

After fielding the complaints and moans such a goal elicits, good leaders collaborate with the team to seek creative solutions that have remained obscured by everyone’s self-limiting beliefs and expectations. To achieve out-of-the-box thinking, sometimes leaders must burn the box.
